title: The Gaussian Channel
description: The capacity of band-limited channels with Gaussian noise, the trade between bandwidth and power, and the Shannon limit on Eb/N0.

study.title: The Gaussian channel
study.body: Many links are well described by $Y = X + Z$: the received sample is the sent one plus Gaussian noise of power $N$, with the transmit power limited to $P$. Its capacity per sample has a closed form, reached with Gaussian-distributed inputs. Unlike the discrete channels before, the 'alphabet' is continuous; the power limit is what keeps the capacity finite.

study.title: Band-limited channels: Shannon–Hartley
study.body: A channel of bandwidth $B$ carries $2B$ independent samples per second, and white noise of density $N_0$ gives a noise power $N = N_0B$. Together this gives the Shannon–Hartley capacity in bit/s. $S/N$ is a power **ratio**: 20 dB means 100. Example: $B$ = 1 MHz at 20 dB gives $C$ = $10^6$ × $\log_2 101$ = 6.66 Mbit/s.

study.title: Explore: bandwidth versus power
study.body: With fixed received power, extra bandwidth also lets in extra noise. Here $P/N_0$ = $10^6$ Hz (60 dB-Hz). At small $B$ the S/N is high and capacity grows almost in proportion to $B$; at large $B$ the S/N drops below 0 dB and capacity saturates at $1.44\,P/N_0$ = 1.44 Mbit/s. Drag $B$ over four decades.

study.title: Spectral efficiency and Eb/N0
study.body: The **spectral efficiency** $\eta = R/B$ measures how well a system uses bandwidth. The fair way to compare power use is the energy per bit over the noise density, $E_b/N_0$: the received power is $P = E_bR$, so $S/N = (E_b/N_0)\,\eta$. Setting $R = C$ in Shannon–Hartley gives the least $E_b/N_0$ that any system with spectral efficiency $\eta$ can use.

study.title: Explore: the Shannon limit
study.body: Plot spectral efficiency against $E_b/N_0$: every real system sits to the right of the Shannon curve. Above $\eta$ = 1 systems are **bandwidth-limited** (bandwidth is the scarce resource, use dense constellations); below it they are **power-limited** (spend bandwidth, e.g. low-rate codes). As $\eta \to 0$ the bound falls to $\ln 2$ = 0.693 = **−1.59 dB**: below that no system works at any rate. Uncoded BPSK/QPSK need 9.6 dB for BER $10^{-5}$; turbo and LDPC codes come within about 1 dB of the limit. Drag $\eta$.

study.title: Explore: BER curves and coding gain
study.body: Uncoded BPSK on the AWGN channel has $P_b = Q(\sqrt{2E_b/N_0})$; QPSK has the same curve per bit. Plotted on a log scale against $E_b/N_0$ in dB, a good code shifts the curve to the left. The **coding gain** is that horizontal shift at a chosen BER: the transmit power saved for the same error rate. Drag $E_b/N_0$.

study.title: Worked example: a satellite transponder
study.body:
$B$ = 36 MHz and $S/N$ = 10 dB (a ratio of 10).
- Capacity: $C$ = 36 MHz × $\log_2 11$ = 124.5 Mbit/s.
- Spectral efficiency at capacity: $\eta$ = 3.46 bit/s/Hz: bandwidth-limited.
- $E_b/N_0 = (S/N)/\eta$ = 10 / 3.46 = 2.89 = 4.6 dB, exactly the Shannon bound for $\eta$ = 3.46.
Doubling the power (13 dB) would add about 34 Mbit/s; doubling the bandwidth at the same power would raise $C$ to 2 × 36 MHz × $\log_2 6$ = 186 Mbit/s.

steps.title: Signal plus Gaussian noise
steps.body: The additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel adds independent Gaussian noise of power $N$ to every transmitted sample, whose power is limited to $P$. Its capacity per sample depends only on the ratio $P/N$.

steps.prompt: Samples sent over an AWGN channel arrive with a signal-to-noise ratio of {{snr}} dB. What is the capacity per sample?

steps.title: Bandwidth: 2B samples per second
steps.body: A signal of bandwidth $B$ is described by $2B$ samples per second, and white noise of density $N_0$ (W/Hz) contributes $N = N_0B$ in that band. Multiplying the per-sample capacity by $2B$ gives the Shannon–Hartley formula.

steps.prompt: A receiver gets {{Pp}} pW of signal power in a bandwidth of {{B|Hz}}. The noise density is $N_0 = 4.0\times 10^{-21}$ W/Hz (thermal noise at room temperature). What is the channel capacity?
A channel has a bandwidth of {{B|Hz}} and an S/N of {{snr}} dB. What is its Shannon capacity?
steps.explanation: Convert first: $S/N = 10^{ {{snr}}/10}$ = {{10^(snr/10)||3}}. $C$ = {{B|Hz}} × $\log_2$({{1 + 10^(snr/10)||4}}) = **{{B*log2(1 + 10^(snr/10))|bit/s}}**. Using {{snr}} as if it were a ratio, $\log_{10}$ instead of $\log_2$, or $2B$ (which belongs with the per-sample form $\tfrac12\log_2$) give the wrong values.

steps.prompt: Doubling the bandwidth of a link at the same received power doubles its capacity.
steps.explanation: False. The noise power $N_0B$ doubles too, so the S/N halves: $C = 2B\log_2(1 + \tfrac{S/N}{2})$. At high S/N that is somewhat less than double; at low S/N it hardly helps at all, because capacity then approaches the limit $1.44\,P/N_0$.

steps.prompt: A {{B|Hz}} channel must carry {{eta*B|bit/s}}. What S/N (in dB) is needed at least?

steps.title: More bandwidth, more noise
steps.body: At fixed received power $P$, widening the band raises the sample rate but lowers the S/N. Capacity keeps growing with $B$ but saturates: it never exceeds $1.44\,P/N_0$. Drag $B$ ($P/N_0$ = $10^6$ Hz here).

steps.prompt: A deep-space link has $P/N_0$ = {{pn}} dB-Hz (i.e. $P/N_0 = 10^{ {{pn}}/10}$ Hz). What is its capacity with unlimited bandwidth?
steps.explanation: $P/N_0$ = {{10^(pn/10)|Hz}}. $C_\infty = (P/N_0)\log_2 e$ = {{10^(pn/10)|Hz}} × 1.443 = **{{10^(pn/10)/ln(2)|bit/s}}**. No amount of bandwidth gives more; only more power (or less noise) does.

steps.prompt: A link runs at an S/N of {{snr}} dB. Its bandwidth is doubled while the received power stays the same. By what factor does the capacity grow?
steps.explanation: $S/N$ = {{10^(snr/10)||3}} becomes {{10^(snr/10)/2||3}}. Ratio = $\frac{2\log_2(1 + {{10^(snr/10)/2||3}})}{\log_2(1 + {{10^(snr/10)||3}})}$ = **{{2*log2(1 + 10^(snr/10)/2)/log2(1 + 10^(snr/10))||3}}**. At high S/N bandwidth is what limits you (factor close to 2); at low S/N it hardly matters (factor close to 1).

steps.title: Two regimes
steps.body: **Power-limited** (low S/N, $\eta$ < 1 bit/s/Hz): $C \approx 1.44\,P/N_0$ grows in proportion to power and hardly depends on $B$; think deep-space probes. **Bandwidth-limited** (high S/N, $\eta$ > 1): $C \approx B\log_2(S/N)$ grows in proportion to $B$, and every extra 3 dB of power adds only about 1 bit/s per Hz; think cable modems and Wi-Fi.

steps.prompt: A {{B|Hz}} link runs at an S/N of {{snr}} dB. How much capacity does doubling the transmit power add?
steps.explanation: $\Delta C = B\log_2\frac{1 + 2S/N}{1 + S/N}$ = {{B|Hz}} × $\log_2$({{(1 + 2*10^(snr/10))/(1 + 10^(snr/10))||4}}) = **{{B*log2((1 + 2*10^(snr/10))/(1 + 10^(snr/10)))|bit/s}}**. At high S/N this approaches $B$ × 1 bit/s/Hz = {{B|bit/s}}; doubling the bandwidth instead would add far more.

steps.prompt: A link works close to capacity at an S/N of {{snr}} dB. In which regime is it?
steps.explanation: At capacity $\eta = \log_2(1 + S/N)$ = $\log_2(1 + {{10^(snr/10)||3}})$ = {{log2(1 + 10^(snr/10))||3}} bit/s/Hz. The boundary $\eta$ = 1 lies at $S/N$ = 1 (0 dB): above it bandwidth is the scarce resource, below it power is.

steps.prompt: With $P/N_0$ = $10^6$ Hz, drag the bandwidth until the capacity reaches {{100*f}} % of its infinite-bandwidth limit.
steps.explanation: $C/C_\infty = x\ln(1 + 1/x)$ with $x = BN_0/P$. It reaches {{100*f}} % at $x$ ≈ {{xs||3}}, i.e. $B$ ≈ **{{xs*1000000|Hz}}** (S/N = {{-10*log10(xs)||2}} dB). Going further buys little: the last {{100 - 100*f}} % would need an infinite bandwidth.

steps.prompt: With unlimited bandwidth, even a weak signal could carry an unlimited bit rate.
steps.explanation: False. As $B \to \infty$ the S/N goes to zero and $C$ approaches $1.44\,P/N_0$, a finite limit set by the received power. That is why deep-space links need big antennas and very low-noise receivers, not just wide bands.

steps.title: The Shannon limit in the efficiency plane
steps.body: With $S/N = (E_b/N_0)\eta$ and $R = C$, Shannon–Hartley gives the least $E_b/N_0$ for each spectral efficiency $\eta$. Real systems lie to the right of this curve. Drag $\eta$ and read the minimum $E_b/N_0$.

steps.prompt: What is the minimum $E_b/N_0$ (in dB) for reliable transmission at a spectral efficiency of {{eta}} bit/s/Hz?
A modem delivers {{eta}} bit/s/Hz at an S/N of {{snr}} dB. What is its $E_b/N_0$ in dB?
As the spectral efficiency goes to zero, the bound $(2^\eta - 1)/\eta$ tends to $\ln 2$. What is that ultimate Shannon limit in dB?
steps.explanation: $10\log_{10}(\ln 2) = 10\log_{10}(0.693)$ = **−1.59 dB**. No system, however much bandwidth it uses, works reliably below this $E_b/N_0$.

steps.prompt: A modem claims {{eta}} bit/s/Hz at $E_b/N_0$ = {{x}} dB with a very low error rate. According to Shannon, this claim is impossible.
steps.explanation: The bound for $\eta$ = {{eta}} is $10\log_{10}\frac{2^{ {{eta}} } - 1}{ {{eta}} }$ = {{10*log10((2^(eta) - 1)/(eta))||3}} dB. A claim **below** the bound is impossible; here the claim is {{x}} dB.

steps.prompt: At $E_b/N_0$ = {{x}} dB, drag the spectral efficiency $\eta$ to the highest value that Shannon allows.
steps.explanation: The bound $(2^\eta - 1)/\eta = 10^{ {{x}}/10}$ = {{10^(x/10)||3}} is met at $\eta$ ≈ **{{es||3}} bit/s/Hz**. Any more bits per hertz would need more $E_b/N_0$.

steps.prompt: A link has $P/N_0$ = {{pn}} dB-Hz and sends {{Rb|bit/s}} in a bandwidth of {{Rb/eta|Hz}}.

ask.prompt: How many dB above the Shannon limit for its spectral efficiency does it operate?
ask.explanation: $\eta$ = {{eta}} bit/s/Hz, so the limit is {{10*log10((2^(eta) - 1)/(eta))||3}} dB. $E_b/N_0$ = {{pn}} − {{10*log10(Rb)||4}} = {{eb||3}} dB. Margin = **{{eb - 10*log10((2^(eta) - 1)/(eta))||3}} dB**: room for a practical modem and code.

steps.prompt: Match each spectral efficiency to the minimum $E_b/N_0$ that Shannon allows.
steps.explanation: $(2^\eta - 1)/\eta$: 1 → 0 dB, 3/2 → 1.76 dB, 15/4 → 5.74 dB, 255/8 → 15.0 dB, and $\ln 2$ → −1.59 dB in the limit. Each extra bit/s/Hz costs more and more energy per bit.

steps.title: Bit error rate curves
steps.body: Uncoded BPSK has a bit error rate $Q(\sqrt{2E_b/N_0})$. On a log scale it falls ever more steeply; BER $10^{-5}$ needs 9.6 dB, about 11 dB from the ultimate limit. Codes move the curve to the left. Drag $E_b/N_0$.

steps.prompt: What is the bit error rate of uncoded BPSK at $E_b/N_0$ = {{x}} dB?
Assume ideal Nyquist pulses, so $M$-ary modulation reaches $\eta = \log_2 M$ bit/s/Hz.

ask.prompt: Uncoded BPSK needs 9.59 dB for BER $10^{-5}$. How far (in dB) is that from the Shannon limit at its spectral efficiency?
ask.explanation: BPSK: $\eta$ = 1, where the limit is $(2^1 - 1)/1$ = 1 = 0 dB. Gap = 9.59 − 0 = **9.59 dB**: a good code can save most of that.

ask.prompt: Uncoded 16-QAM needs 13.4 dB for BER $10^{-5}$. How far (in dB) is that from the Shannon limit at its spectral efficiency?
Uncoded 64-QAM needs 17.8 dB for BER $10^{-5}$. How far (in dB) is that from the Shannon limit at its spectral efficiency?

steps.prompt: Uncoded BPSK needs 9.6 dB for BER $10^{-5}$. With a channel code the same BER is reached at {{x}} dB (both $E_b/N_0$ per information bit).

ask.explanation: Coding gain = horizontal shift at the target BER = 9.6 − {{x}} = **{{9.6 - x||3}} dB**.

ask.prompt: By what factor can the transmit power be reduced (same bit rate)?
ask.explanation: Gain {{9.6 - x||3}} dB → factor $10^{ {{9.6 - x||3}}/10}$ = **{{10^((9.6 - x)/10)||3}}**. That can mean a smaller antenna, a longer range or a longer battery life.

steps.prompt: BPSK with a rate-{{r}} code has a spectral efficiency of $\eta$ = {{r}} bit/s/Hz (ideal pulses). What is the Shannon limit on $E_b/N_0$ for that efficiency?
steps.explanation: $\frac{2^{ {{r}} } - 1}{ {{r}} }$ = {{(2^r - 1)/r||3}} = **{{10*log10((2^(r) - 1)/(r))||3}} dB**. Lower-rate codes buy a lower limit with bandwidth: below $\eta$ = 1 every system is power-limited.

steps.prompt: From the graph of uncoded BPSK, read the $E_b/N_0$ needed for a bit error rate of $10^{-{{k}}}$.
steps.explanation: The curve crosses $10^{-{{k}}}$ at about **{{if(abs(k - 3) - 0.5, if(abs(k - 4) - 0.5, if(abs(k - 5) - 0.5, 10.53, 9.59), 8.40), 6.79)}} dB** ($Q(\sqrt{2E_b/N_0}) = 10^{-{{k}}}$). Each decade of BER costs about 1.6 dB around $10^{-3}$ but under 1 dB near $10^{-6}$: the curve keeps getting steeper.

steps.prompt: A deep-space probe arrives with $P/N_0$ = {{pn}} dB-Hz. Its code needs $E_b/N_0$ = {{x}} dB. What is the highest bit rate it can support?
steps.explanation: $E_b/N_0 = (P/N_0)/R_b$ → $R_b = (P/N_0)/(E_b/N_0)$, in dB: {{pn}} − {{x}} = {{pn - x}} dB-bit/s → $R_b = 10^{ {{(pn - x)/10}} }$ = **{{10^((pn - x)/10)|bit/s}}**. Each dB saved by better coding raises the rate by 26 %.

steps.prompt: A new code that reaches BER $10^{-5}$ at $E_b/N_0$ = −2 dB would be a breakthrough worth publishing.
steps.explanation: False: it cannot exist. Below $\ln 2$ = −1.59 dB no system communicates reliably at any spectral efficiency, however long its codewords. A measurement like that points to a calibration error.
